abstract:
Human intestinal
permeability is a key determinant of the oral
fraction absorbed ( f a ) of active pharmaceutical
ingredients (APIs). This study evaluated the ability of an in-house
canine Mdr1 (cMdr1) knockout (KO) Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK)
cell line to correlate in vitro apparent permeability
( P app ) with human small intestinal permeability
( P eff ). In vitro P app values of 16 reference compounds with high,
medium, or low permeabilities were measured in the in-house cMdr1
KO MDCK protocol under pH gradient (6.5 ⇒ 7.4) and pH equivalent
conditions (7.4 ⇒ 7.4) and correlations with human P eff were established ( R 2 > 0.8). The correlations were subsequently used to estimate P eff and f a for six
test APIs: acetaminophen, voriconazole, fedratinib, voxelotor, lemborexant,
and istradefylline. The results for these APIs were compared against
literature and permeability data from other methods routinely used
in drug discovery and development. The projected P eff and f a values for the
test APIs aligned well with literature permeabilities derived using
other methods and clinical pharmacokinetic studies, respectively.
This work highlights the usefulness of cMdr1 KO MDCK cells in permeability
classification, especially for highly permeable APIs, and supports
its broader use in both research and regulatory contexts.

Literature Review
Online literature

perfusion studies and their results (human

where available: number of subjects, prandial state, perfusion technique,
intestinal segment perfused, perfusate composition, perfusion rate,
perfusion duration, aspiration intervals, measures of API stability
in the perfusate, and API adsorption to the perfusion catheters. The

small intestine during clinical BA studies.

The selection criteria for

Selection criteria encompassed characteristics of the compounds as

The following aspects were considered:
(i)
Selected compounds
should represent
low, medium, and high permeability.
(ii)
The permeation mechanism should be
passive diffusion.
(iii)
Compounds should be metabolically
stable in the small intestine.
(iv)
The percentage of ionization should

(v)
Preferably, compounds should be included

A set

from Caco-2 cell monolayer permeability experiments and literature

P

Six APIs (acetaminophen, voriconazole, fedratinib, voxelotor, lemborexant
and istradefylline), previously studied by Beran et al., were selected.
3.4
Chemicals and Reagents
The following
16 reference compounds were obtained from J&J compound management
or purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA): amiloride, antipyrine,
[3H]-atenolol, carbamazepine, cimetidine, desipramine, fluvastatin,
furosemide, inogatran, ketoprofen, metoprolol, naproxen, piroxicam,
[3H]-propranolol, ranitidine, and terbutaline.
The six test
APIs were purchased from Merck Life Science BV (Overijse, Belgium),
Biosynth Carbosynth (Compton, UK), or MedChemExpress LLC (Monmouth
Junction, NJ, USA).
Cell culture
reagents were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific
(Waltham, MA, USA).
3.5
Canine Mdr1 Knockout in
MDCK Wildtype Cells
by CRISPR-CAS9 Technology
MDCK parental cells were sourced
from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, CCL-34, Manassas,
VA, USA). This parental cell line exhibits a transepithelial electrical
resistance (TEER) of approximately 1000 Ω·cm
2
(measured in-house).
The endogenous cMdr1 gene was knocked
out using CRISPR-CAS9 technology.
,
The MDCK wildtype
cells were transfected with a mixture of TrueCut Cas9 protein V2 (Thermo
Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA),
in vitro
transcribed
guide RNA (gRNA) targeting the cMdr1 gene, and a DNA oligo donor that
introduced an in-frame stop codon by electroporation. The targeted
genomic region was exon 3 and the gRNA sequence (5′ to 3′)
was ATAG­GTTG­TATA­TGTT­GGTG. Genomic cleavage
was assessed 72 h post-transfection using the GeneArt Cleavage Detection
kit (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). The transfected cells were
sorted by flow cytometry for clonal selection and expansion. Gene
deletion was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of the targeted genomic
region. The selected clone (MDCK KO) was further transduced with a
control lentiviral construct containing a puromycin resistance marker,
followed by selection with puromycin and subsequent monoclonal selection
using a single cell clonal dilution method (MDCK KO empty vector (EV)).
Functional efflux activity of known P-gp substrates was evaluated
in both MDCK KO and MDCK KO EV clones and compared with MDCK wildtype.
The MDCK KO EV cells were used in the API transport studies reported
here.
3.6
Cell Culture and Plating
The cMdr1
KO MDCK cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s
Medium (DMEM), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100
units/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 1 μg/mL
puromycin. All cells were grown at 37 °C, 5% CO
2
,
and 90% relative humidity and subcultured using trypsin-EDTA (0.25%)
solution as a dissociation reagent.
All experiments were conducted
using cells between passages 4 and 13, and no systematic differences
in the permeability of positive controls were observed. The cells
were plated at a seeding density of 340,000 cells/cm
2
on
porous membrane inserts (Millicell 96-well, 0.4 μm pore size,
MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA) and cultured in the absence of puromycin
for 4 days at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO
2
.
3.7
Permeability Studies
The permeabilities
of the reference compounds and test APIs across cultured monolayers
of cMdr1 KO MDCK cell monolayers were measured 4 days after plating.
The studies included determination of drug permeability in absorptive
direction (apical to basolateral side (A⇒B)) as well as in
secretive direction (basolateral to apical side (B⇒A)). The
impact of pH on drug permeability was assessed within the pH range
of 6.5 to 7.4, by either employing a pH gradient (pH 6.5 on the apical
side and pH 7.4 on the basolateral side) or maintaining a constant
pH of 7.4 in both compartments.
Hank’s Balanced Salt
Solution (HBSS), supplemented with 25 mM HEPES (4-(2-Hydroxyethyl)­piperazine-1-ethanesulfonic
acid) and 25 mM glucose, served as the transport buffer. The investigated
drugs were prepared at 1 μM in HBSS containing the cell monolayer
integrity marker lucifer yellow at a concentration of 100 μM
(dosing solution). Compound stock solutions in dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) were spiked into the transport buffer, maintaining a DMSO concentration
of ≤ 0.3% v/v. The receiver solutions were blank transport
buffer containing DMSO at a concentration equal to that used in the
dosing solution.
In preparation of the experiments, the cell
monolayers were washed
twice with prewarmed transport buffer, and the plates were equilibrated
in transport buffer for 40 min at 37 °C.
The permeability
experiments were performed on three different
occasions, with all permeabilities measured in triplicate (
n
= 3) on each occasion. The dosing solutions containing
the investigated drug were added to the donor compartments, followed
by addition of the receiver solution to the corresponding receiver
compartments. The volume added to both apical and basolateral compartments
was 0.15 mL. The plates were incubated for 90 min at 37 °C on
a shaking incubator at 120 rpm (Model MaxQ 4000, Barnstead, Melrose
Park, IL, USA).
At the end of the incubation, top and bottom
plates were separated,
and samples were taken from both the donor and receiver compartments.
Aliquots were also taken from the dosing vials for determination of
the initial concentration upon administration. The concentrations
of unlabeled APIs were quantified using liquid chromatography with
tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), while radiolabeled compounds
were quantified using liquid scintillation counting (LSC). The lucifer
yellow concentrations were quantified by measuring fluorescence intensity
using a plate reader. Details about the methods for sample analysis
are provided in the

For the permeability studies with the test APIs, atenolol
and propranolol

in each test.

body:
1
Introduction
Permeability is a key biopharmaceutical property of active pharmaceutical
ingredients (APIs), characterizing their ability to traverse biological
barriers. In the context of oral drug absorption, permeability across
the intestinal epithelium determines the transport rate of APIs from
the intestinal lumen into the portal vein and is thus a major driver
of oral fraction absorbed (
f
a
) and bioavailability
(BA). Investigating intestinal drug permeability early in discovery
is therefore essential for evaluating and comparing the biopharmaceutical
properties of APIs with respect to oral absorption, supporting selection
of promising API candidates and guiding their formulation development.
The significance of permeability also extends to regulatory filings,
postapproval changes and generic drug approval.
,
In its original version, the Biopharmaceutics Classification System
(BCS) classified the permeability of APIs based on pharmacokinetic
(PK) studies in humans, using absolute oral BA or mass balance study
results to determine the
f
a
after oral
administration.
−
To distinguish between highly and poorly permeable
APIs, the BCS employed a cutoff of 90% for the
f
a
.
Later, the cutoff was reduced
to 85% absorption and an option to classify permeability based on
data from validated Caco-2 cell models was added.
The use of validated cell models facilitates permeability
classification prior to running PK studies in humans. In this approach,
the apparent permeability (
P
app
) of the
investigational API is determined
in vitro
and compared
to
P
app
values of reference compounds
with known
f
a
in humans.
Permeability classification in the Developability
Classification
System (DCS) and its evolution, the refined Developability Classification
System (rDCS), is based on estimates of human small intestinal permeability
(
P
eff
), which is often referred to as
the “gold standard”.
−
P
eff
represents a quantitative measure of permeability, reflecting
the net velocity of drug transport across the epithelium.
,
P
eff
is typically expressed as distance
per time in cm/s. Applications of
P
eff
include the calculation of the maximum absorbable dose (MAD) and
the solubility-limited absorbable dose (SLAD) in the DCS and rDCS.
−
,
Furthermore,
P
eff
is used as the permeability input in Physiologically
Based Biopharmaceutics Modeling (PBBM) and Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetics
Modeling (PBPK).
,
Human
P
eff
can be determined
in vivo
through
single-pass intestinal perfusion studies.
,
Following perfusion of an intestinal test segment,
P
eff
is calculated as the luminal clearance (CL) of the
API per intestinal surface area.
While
direct determination of
P
eff
via human
intestinal perfusion would appear to be the most reliable approach,
several issues are associated with this method. These include patient
welfare during the clinical procedure,
practical difficulties such as the intubation procedure and correct
tube positioning, low throughput, high resource and time demands,
selection of relevant experimental conditions and the methodology
applied to data analysis.
,
Most importantly, human
intubation methods are obviously not an option for permeability assessment
in the discovery and preclinical stage.
Thus, alternative methods
for
P
eff
determination
involve estimation using surrogate techniques, such as preclinical
in vivo
studies (e.g., rodent PK studies),
in situ
perfusion studies in preclinical species (e.g., rat intestinal perfusion
studies),
ex vivo
transport models (e.g., Ussing
chamber technique),
in vitro
cellular transport models
(e.g., Caco-2 or Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cell models), and
in vitro
noncellular transport models (e.g., Parallel Artificial
Membrane Permeability Assays (PAMPA)).
,
In
silico
approaches include quantitative structure property
relationships (QSPR), aimed at correlating molecular descriptors with
permeability.
Additionally, a bottom-up
mechanistic permeability model (“MechPeff”) for the
prediction of regional intestinal passive permeability has been developed,
integrating physicochemical properties of the API and physiological/anatomical
parameters.
Details of the different
methods have been described in recent reviews.
,
Since pharmaceutical research and development is increasingly shaped
by ethical considerations and sustainability, greater focus should
be directed toward advancing animal-free approaches. When utilizing
surrogate techniques, a robust correlation between data from the surrogate
method and
in vivo
permeability values is needed
to project the human
P
eff
value of a given
API. Best practices for the estimation of human jejunal
P
eff
(particularly for PBBM) have recently been discussed
in a workshop organized by the University of Maryland Center of Excellence
in Regulatory Science and Innovation (M-CERSI) and the Food and Drug
Administration (FDA).
Most participants
revealed that they rely on data from transport studies using cultured
epithelial cells (e.g., Caco-2 or MDCK cells). These
in vitro
data are typically converted to
P
eff
using in-house calibration curves. Literature correlations, including
the internal correlations embedded in commercially available software,
are less frequently employed. It was further noted that
P
eff
estimations can be optimized as oral solution PK data
become available during clinical development.
Both Caco-2 and
MDCK cell models have been demonstrated to correlate
with human intestinal absorption.
However,
the significantly shorter culture times for MDCK cells (3–7
days) compared to Caco-2 cells (14–28 days) enable higher throughput,
making them particularly advantageous for API screening in discovery.
Since MDCK cell models are widely used across
the industry, there was a consensus among industry participants in
a separate M-CERSI/FDA workshop on drug permeability that regulatory
guidelines should consider MDCK data more broadly, including its use
as supportive evidence for BCS permeability classification.
In this context, permeability classifications
based on a “totality-of-evidence” approach, utilizing
permeability data from two or more methods, was considered to derive
more robust permeability classifications.
As an example of supportive evidence, Varma et al. utilized low
endogenous efflux MDCK cells for high-throughput API permeability
screening to assign provisional biopharmaceutics classifications.
In this study, we used an in-house, genetically
engineered canine
P-Glycoprotein (cMdr1) knockout (KO) MDCK cell line to measure the
permeability of selected reference compounds, aiming to establish
a robust
P
app
–
P
eff
correlation. Additionally, a correlation between
P
app
and
f
a
was built.
The cMdr1 knockout was implemented to eliminate confounding effects
from the endogenous canine efflux transporter, enabling a better focus
on passive permeation through the cell monolayers. Thus, the resulting
correlations are most relevant for estimating the human intestinal
permeability of passively absorbed APIs, with a view to early BCS/rDCS
classification in discovery, as an input for PBBM, and as part of
a “totality-of-evidence” approach to formal BCS/rDCS
classification. To identify suitable reference compounds for the correlation,
a thorough literature review was conducted. The resulting correlation
was subsequently used to estimate the
P
eff
of six test APIs. The results were compared to
P
eff
estimates derived through other methods, including
Caco-2 cell transport studies.
Additionally,
f
a
estimates based on the permeability data were
compared with the results of literature pharmacokinetic studies.
2
Literature Human Permeability Data Repositories
The
reference human
P
eff
data used
to build
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations comes primarily from studies conducted
at Uppsala University and the University of Michigan. Compilations
of
P
eff
values are available in literature
reviews. For instance, Avdeef and Tam listed and analyzed 119
P
eff
values for 53 substances, 34 of which can
be considered small-molecule APIs.
Dahlgren
et al. compiled 273
P
eff
values of 80
substances, 39 of which can be considered small-molecule APIs.
Rosenberger et al. published a compilation of
63 compounds with either known human
P
eff
or predicted
P
eff
values based on rat
data, with 54 of the substances considered to be small-molecule APIs.
In addition, these data repositories include
P
eff
values of polyethylene glycols (PEGs), monosaccharides,
amino acids, alkane acids, bile acids, inorganic ions, and water.
When building an in-house
P
app
–
P
eff
correlation, reference compounds and their
corresponding human
P
eff
data should be
carefully selected from these data repositories, keeping certain criteria
in mind. For example, if the goal is to estimate human permeability
of small-molecule APIs, the correlation should include reference compounds
with comparable chemical properties but exclude substances such as
PEGs, inorganic ions, or water. Furthermore, the correlation should
be limited to passively absorbed APIs, since inclusion of compounds
known to be absorbed or excreted via transporters has been shown to
produce poor correlations.
,
A major concern
with the published results of human perfusion studies
is the frequent lack of transparency and consistency in the study
designs and experimental conditions. Human intestinal perfusion studies
have often been designed to assess the impact of specific experimental
variables on the
in vivo
permeability of APIs, such
as coadministration with other drugs, excipients or nutrients, pretreatment
with other drugs, variations in the perfusate composition (e.g., the
osmolarity), or variations in the perfusion rate. Frequently, perfusion
experiments have been conducted on multiple occasions within one study
and/or the perfusion period was split into several segments, varying
specific experimental parameters.
,
Critical factors
that can affect the resulting
P
eff
, including
the perfusion technique, location of perfusion in the gut, composition
of the perfusate, and methods for data evaluation, should therefore
be thoroughly assessed before including
P
eff
values in the reference set for the correlation. In this work, we
conducted a comprehensive literature review, compiling both the
P
eff
values and the attendant experimental conditions.
This review served as a robust basis for defining appropriate inclusion
and exclusion criteria, in alignment with the study aims.
3
Materials and Methods
3.1
Literature Review
Online literature
databases were systematically reviewed for reports on human intestinal
perfusion studies and their results (human
P
eff
). The following experimental parameters were collected
where available: number of subjects, prandial state, perfusion technique,
intestinal segment perfused, perfusate composition, perfusion rate,
perfusion duration, aspiration intervals, measures of API stability
in the perfusate, and API adsorption to the perfusion catheters. The
reported
P
eff
(±SD) and the percentage
recovery of the nonabsorbable marker included in the perfusate (usually
PEG4000) were also noted, if available. In total, 37 studies were
reviewed. The experimental conditions and results were assessed for
their consistency and relevance to the conditions present in the human
small intestine during clinical BA studies.
3.2
Compound
Selection: Reference Compounds
The selection criteria for
reference compounds to be included in
the
P
app
–
P
eff
correlation were defined based on the literature review.
Selection criteria encompassed characteristics of the compounds as
well as the experimental conditions for
P
eff
determination.
The following aspects were considered:
(i)
Selected compounds
should represent
low, medium, and high permeability.
(ii)
The permeation mechanism should be
passive diffusion.
(iii)
Compounds should be metabolically
stable in the small intestine.
(iv)
The percentage of ionization should
be similar under pH conditions of 6.5 to 7.4.
(v)
Preferably, compounds should be included
in the ICH M9 Guideline’s list of permeability references.
As different pH
conditions close to pH 7 have been used in both
in vitro
and
in vivo
studies, the API’s
ionization behavior is an important consideration. If the p
K
a
is close to or falls within the range of 6.5
to 7.4, the API may exhibit varying ionization states under these
conditions. A change in ionization can have an influence on the API’s
apparent permeability. For example, different apparent permeability
values have been observed for fedratinib in Caco-2 cells at pH 6.5
and 7.4,
highlighting the need to consider
ionization when evaluating drug permeability.
Additionally,
the following experimental conditions for human intestinal
perfusion studies were considered as inclusion criteria to ensure
a reliable and consistent set of
P
eff
values:
(vi)
Use of the Loc-I-Gut
technique.
(vii)
Perfusion
of the proximal small
intestine.
(viii)

rate between 2–3
mL/min.
(ix)
Documentation
of the perfusate composition,
including drug concentration, pH and osmolarity. The drug concentration
should preferably be therapeutically relevant, the pH should be between
6.5 and 7.4 and the perfusate should be isotonic.
(x)
Reporting of the number of subjects
(preferably high) and standard deviations.
(xi)
Reporting of the PEG4000 recovery
(preferably high).
(xii)
Documentation of API stability in
the perfusate, and absence of significant adsorption onto the perfusion

A set

[3H]-atenolol, carbamazepine, cimetidine, desipramine, fluvastatin,

The six test

Cell culture

3.5
Canine Mdr1 Knockout in
MDCK Wildtype Cells
by CRISPR-CAS9 Technology
MDCK parental cells were sourced
from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, CCL-34, Manassas,
VA, USA). This parental cell line exhibits a transepithelial electrical
resistance (TEER) of approximately 1000 Ω·cm
2
(measured in-house).
The endogenous cMdr1 gene was knocked
out using CRISPR-CAS9 technology.
,
The MDCK wildtype
cells were transfected with a mixture of TrueCut Cas9 protein V2 (Thermo
Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA),
in vitro
transcribed
guide RNA (gRNA) targeting the cMdr1 gene, and a DNA oligo donor that
introduced an in-frame stop codon by electroporation. The targeted
genomic region was exon 3 and the gRNA sequence (5′ to 3′)
was ATAG­GTTG­TATA­TGTT­GGTG. Genomic cleavage
was assessed 72 h post-transfection using the GeneArt Cleavage Detection
kit (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). The transfected cells were
sorted by flow cytometry for clonal selection and expansion. Gene
deletion was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of the targeted genomic
region. The selected clone (MDCK KO) was further transduced with a
control lentiviral construct containing a puromycin resistance marker,
followed by selection with puromycin and subsequent monoclonal selection
using a single cell clonal dilution method (MDCK KO empty vector (EV)).
Functional efflux activity of known P-gp substrates was evaluated
in both MDCK KO and MDCK KO EV clones and compared with MDCK wildtype.
The MDCK KO EV cells were used in the API transport studies reported
here.
3.6
Cell Culture and Plating
The cMdr1
KO MDCK cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s
Medium (DMEM), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100
units/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 1 μg/mL
puromycin. All cells were grown at 37 °C, 5% CO
2
,
and 90% relative humidity and subcultured using trypsin-EDTA (0.25%)
solution as a dissociation reagent.
All experiments were conducted
using cells between passages 4 and 13, and no systematic differences
in the permeability of positive controls were observed. The cells
were plated at a seeding density of 340,000 cells/cm
2
on
porous membrane inserts (Millicell 96-well, 0.4 μm pore size,
MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA) and cultured in the absence of puromycin
for 4 days at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO
2
.
3.7
Permeability Studies
The permeabilities
of the reference compounds and test APIs across cultured monolayers
of cMdr1 KO MDCK cell monolayers were measured 4 days after plating.
The studies included determination of drug permeability in absorptive
direction (apical to basolateral side (A⇒B)) as well as in
secretive direction (basolateral to apical side (B⇒A)). The
impact of pH on drug permeability was assessed within the pH range
of 6.5 to 7.4, by either employing a pH gradient (pH 6.5 on the apical
side and pH 7.4 on the basolateral side) or maintaining a constant
pH of 7.4 in both compartments.
Hank’s Balanced Salt
Solution (HBSS), supplemented with 25 mM HEPES (4-(2-Hydroxyethyl)­piperazine-1-ethanesulfonic
acid) and 25 mM glucose, served as the transport buffer. The investigated
drugs were prepared at 1 μM in HBSS containing the cell monolayer
integrity marker lucifer yellow at a concentration of 100 μM
(dosing solution). Compound stock solutions in dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) were spiked into the transport buffer, maintaining a DMSO concentration
of ≤ 0.3% v/v. The receiver solutions were blank transport
buffer containing DMSO at a concentration equal to that used in the
dosing solution.
In preparation of the experiments, the cell
monolayers were washed
twice with prewarmed transport buffer, and the plates were equilibrated
in transport buffer for 40 min at 37 °C.
The permeability
experiments were performed on three different
occasions, with all permeabilities measured in triplicate (
n
= 3) on each occasion. The dosing solutions containing
the investigated drug were added to the donor compartments, followed
by addition of the receiver solution to the corresponding receiver
compartments. The volume added to both apical and basolateral compartments
was 0.15 mL. The plates were incubated for 90 min at 37 °C on
a shaking incubator at 120 rpm (Model MaxQ 4000, Barnstead, Melrose
Park, IL, USA).
At the end of the incubation, top and bottom
plates were separated,
and samples were taken from both the donor and receiver compartments.
Aliquots were also taken from the dosing vials for determination of
the initial concentration upon administration. The concentrations
of unlabeled APIs were quantified using liquid chromatography with
tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), while radiolabeled compounds
were quantified using liquid scintillation counting (LSC). The lucifer
yellow concentrations were quantified by measuring fluorescence intensity
using a plate reader. Details about the methods for sample analysis
are provided in the
Supporting Information
.
For the permeability studies with the test APIs, atenolol
and propranolol
were run separately on individual filters as quality control standards
in each test.

5
Discussion
The use of
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations is a widely accepted method
for estimating
human small intestinal permeability.
The
purpose of these studies was to determine whether cMdr1 KO MDCK cell
monolayers are suitable for establishing
P
app
-based correlations to estimate human
P
eff
and
f
a
of test APIs.
The first
step was to critically evaluate the
P
eff
data reported in the literature, such that only reference
compounds and associated
in vivo
permeability data
that met predefined selection criteria were used to generate the correlations.
The second step was to correlate the in-house generated
in vitro
P
app
data of the selected
reference compounds, obtained at both pH 6.5 ⇒ 7.4 and pH 7.4
⇒ 7.4, to determine whether use of an apical to basolateral
pH gradient improves the correlation.
The third step was to
utilize the correlations based on cMdr1 KO
MDCK cells to estimate
P
eff
and
f
a
for six test APIs and compare the results
with permeability data reported in the literature and
P
eff
estimations obtained through other methods typically
employed in pharmaceutical research and development.
5.1
Evaluating
Literature
P
eff
Data and Selecting Reference
Compounds
A recent
workshop recommended that the reference data set for establishing
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations
includes compounds with high, medium, and low permeability.
Despite the availability of numerous
P
eff
values in the literature, establishing a
set of appropriate reference compounds presented significant challenges.
A major difficulty lies in the frequent lack of transparency and consistency
in the methodologies used for
P
eff
measurement.
Additionally, navigating literature
P
eff
data is often hindered by cross-referencing between publications,
leading to certain “dead ends” where the original sources
of values cannot be traced. Inconsistent reporting formats, varying
levels of methodological detail, and the inaccessibility of certain
studies further complicate the issue. Therefore, selecting
P
eff
values from compiled databases without understanding
their specific context is not a reliable scientific approach.
The issues around
P
eff
data selection,
especially regarding consistency in experimental conditions employed
in human intestinal perfusion studies, are discussed in-depth in the
Supporting Information
. This discussion includes
the number of study participants, test segment location, intraluminal
perfusion technique, perfusion rates, mass transport models for calculating
P
eff
, perfusate composition, API stability and
adsorption to tubing.
Based on the literature review conducted
in this work, a set of
16 reference compounds was assembled. Of the data that are accessible
in the open literature, this set includes the most consistent and
transparent set of permeability data available for establishing
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations.
Low permeability compounds with
f
a
<
50% are underrepresented in the reference set. Inogatran is the only
compound belonging to this category. Thus, the use of this data set
is expected to provide a higher degree of confidence in
P
eff
estimations for moderate-to-high permeability compounds.
5.2
Establishing
P
app
–
P
eff
Correlations in Modified
MDCK Cell Monolayers under Varying pH Conditions
The
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations
established with the 16 reference compounds in cMdr1 KO MDCK cells
consistently achieved
R
2
values greater
than 0.8, regardless of the pH conditions. This aligns with the ionization
behavior of most of the reference compounds, which exhibit similar
fractions ionized at pH 6.5 and 7.4, with only three exceptions: cimetidine,
ranitidine, and inogatran. Generally, while perfusate pH in perfusion
studies range from pH 6.2 and 8.2 in the literature (with most perfusion
studies conducted at either pH 6.5 or 7.4), the
in vivo
relevance of pH-dependent permeability remains unclear, as the impact
of luminal pH on the microclimate pH at the mucosal brush border has
not been well described.
Additionally,
the ability of the small intestine to rapidly adjust pH, along with
the relatively stable pH microclimate in the mucus layer suggest a
limited impact of luminal pH on drug permeability
in vivo
during perfusion studies, as indicated by both rat and human data.
,
Repeatability was within common ranges for
in vitro
permeability experiments. The
P
app
results
within the overall pH 6.5 ⇒ 7.4 and pH 7.4 ⇒ 7.4 data
sets varied by 34% and 26% from the mean
P
app
values, respectively, based on the average coefficient of variation
across the 16 reference compounds.

For voxelotor and istradefylline, no human BA or

The permeability data for voxelotor were regarded

,
However, the
results presented in this work strongly suggest classification as
highly permeable for both voxelotor and istradefylline.
Fedratinib
presents a more complex case, with
P

–4
cm/s. These values cover low, medium, and high permeability
categories, depending on the estimation approach used. The variability
in predictions across various methods complicate a definitive permeability

of each method. The lowest

value
(0.06 × 10
–4
cm/s) was derived from the MechPeff

Notably, method 2 within the MechPeff model, which is also based

and ADMET Predictor, estimate

at
0.22 × 10
–4

–4
cm/s, respectively. It is important to note that these approaches
are less commonly applied than transport studies using epithelial
cell models, because the latter are often assumed to produce more

P

Permeability data from both the Caco-2
model and the cMdr1 KO MDCK
model indicated pH-dependent permeability for fedratinib. Higher
P

has basic p

As the pH shifts from 6.5 to 7.4, a larger monocationic
fraction of fedratinib is present, which is likely more permeable

In the cMdr1 KO MDCK model under pH
6.5 ⇒ 7.4 conditions,
using adjusted

–4
cm/s for pH 6.5 ⇒ 7.4 and 3.05 × 10
–4

revealed further complexity, as

of 0.35 × 10

Mass balance and metabolic profiling studies
for fedratinib estimated
f

values of
65 to 77%,
,
indicating medium permeability
in vivo
. For challenging
cases like fedratinib, the “totality-of-evidence” approach
is particularly useful as it can highlight potential complexities
in permeability, prompting in-depth analysis. Customized studies involving
various models, pH conditions, and concentrations are advisible to
fully characterize fedratinib’s permeability behavior, including
potential BA risks.
Overall, variability of the projected
P
eff
values across experiments ranged between
a coefficient of variation
of 5–12% and 11–16% when using the
P
app
data “as-is” or adjusting the data according
to the reference compounds, respectively. Only the variability for

due to its pH-dependent permeability. Adjustment of the data according
to the reference compounds made little difference to the
P
eff
predictions but seemed to increase the variation among
experiments in a given set. However, due to the low number of results
in each data set (
n

only be interpreted as trends.
Given the variability in permeability
measurements demonstrated
here on an interoccasion basis as well as reported in the literature
on an interlaboratory basis, normalizing
P

Considering the findings for the six test APIs, use of the correlations
established using cMdr1 KO MDCK cells, effectively contributed to
the classification of five APIs as highly permeable using the “totality-of-evidence”
strategy. For fedratinib, this approach helped to reveal and understand
the complexities in its permeation behavior.
Overall, the data
provide strong support for the cMdr1 KO MDCK
model as a valuable tool in identifying highly permeable APIs with
passive permeation mechanism. However, its applicability in the medium-to-low
permeability space still needs to be clarified through further studies.
5.4
Comparison of the MDCK and Caco-2 in Vitro
Systems
Different epithelial cell lines have been used to
build
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations, including Caco-2 cells,
,
MDCK cells,
and LLC-PK1 cells.
While Caco-2 data are most frequently
included in regulatory applications and are recognized for their reliability
in assessing high permeability compounds, the importance to cross-check
permeability results across diverse data sets and
P
eff
estimates obtained through various methodologies has
been highlighted in the literature.
This
approach has been referred to as a “totality-of-evidence”
approach.
MDCK cells offer some advantages over Caco-2 cells
for drug permeability
screening due to their shorter culture times.
,
Different
strains of MDCK cells are available, such as the parental line, type
I, type II and others.
These strains
can differ in their composition of epithelial junctions, TEER values,
cell size and morphology, and apical membrane protein expression.
Based on in-house data, the MDCK II strain
exhibited a TEER value
of around 120 Ω·cm
2
, leading to slightly higher
P
app
values for paracellular markers compared
to the parental MDCK strain, which had a TEER of about 1000 Ω·cm
2
. It is noted that, although the latter TEER was even higher
than that of Caco-2 cells (between 250–350 Ω·cm
2
), the paracellular permeability of marker substances was
similar when comparing parental MDCK cells and Caco-2 cells.
Moreover, since MDCK cells are of canine origin and derived from
kidney tubule epithelial cells, their transporter and enzyme expression
profiles can differ from those of the human intestinal epithelium,
potentially altering permeability characteristics. For instance, MDCK
cells are reported to endogenously express ADME-related renal transporters
such as organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) or organic cation/carnitine
transporter protein 2 (OCTN2).
,
However, major organic
anion transporters (OATs such as OAT1 or OAT3), or multidrug and toxin
extrusion proteins (MATEs such as MATE1 or MATE2-K) have not been
detected in MDCK cells.
,
While the inclusion
criteria for our reference compound selection specified that the permeation
mechanism should be passive diffusion, we acknowledge that the evidence
for transporter involvement is not always definitive or complete.
While we attempted to exclude well-established transporter substrates,
we cannot fully exclude the possibility that some compounds in the
set may interact with renal transporters endogenously expressed in
MDCK cells. Some of the reference compounds (e.g., ranitidine and
cimetidine) have been reported to be substrates of renal OCTs, primarily
in the context of renal clearance.
−
However, their oral
absorption is largely believed to be governed by passive diffusion,
supported by permeability and pharmacokinetic profiling.
,
In contrast to canine derived MDCK cells, Caco-2 cells are
of human
origin, originating from colorectal adenocarcinoma. These cells express
a range of ADME-related drug transporters, including MDR1, BCRP, and
OATP2B1.
Discrepancies in transporter
expression levels between Caco-2 and human intestinal tissues present
challenges in correlating
in vitro
findings with
in vivo
performance for transporter substrates. For example,
the uptake transporter OATP2B1 has been reported to be 16 times more
abundant in Caco-2 cells compared to jejunal tissue.
Nevertheless, both Caco-2 and MDCK-based models have
demonstrated
good correlation with human intestinal absorption parameters. Given
that practical, robust, and widely applicable human small intestinal
cell lines or organoid-derived tissue models are still under development
and evaluation, Caco-2 and MDCK currently provide the most valuable
tools for high-throughput applications.
6
Conclusions
This study outlines a structured approach to establishing in-house
P
app
–
P
eff
correlations,
utilizing a set of 16 carefully selected reference compounds that
span different permeability classes while ensuring consistency in
the experimental conditions used for
in vivo
P
eff
determination (human perfusion studies).
The correlations developed using cMdr1 KO MDCK cells demonstrated
strong fits, with
R
2
values consistently
exceeding 0.8 under varying pH conditions. Since the focus was on
passively permeable APIs and P-gp was knocked out in the MDCK cells,
the correlations are best suited for estimating passive permeability
of test APIs. The MDCK model effectively contributed to identifying
test APIs that are highly permeable, with projected
P
eff
values aligning well with those derived from other
methods and existing literature. However, low permeability APIs, particularly
those listed in ICH M9, were underrepresented, highlighting a potential
gap in the current reference set.
This work emphasizes the usefulness
of cMdr1 KO MDCK cells in permeability
classification, especially for highly permeable APIs. Regulatory guidelines
could benefit from updates to acknowledge the utility of such models
as part of a “totality-of-evidence” approach, reinforcing
their role as supportive evidence in permeability assessments.
